title: Arc Length
body:
The length of a curve, as opposed to the area under it. Straighten a tiny piece of the curve into
its hypotenuse, $ds = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}$, and add up the pieces. That single expression is the
whole topic; the three formulas below are it with different things factored out.

## Three forms, one idea

| Curve given as | Formula |
|---|---|
| $y = f(x)$ on $[a,b]$ | $L = \displaystyle\int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \left[f'(x)\right]^2}\,dx$ |
| [[Parametric Equations\|parametric]] $x(t), y(t)$ on $[\alpha,\beta]$ | $L = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt$ |
| [[Polar Coordinates\|polar]] $r = f(\theta)$ on $[\alpha,\beta]$ | $L = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\tfrac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta$ |

Factor $dx$ out of $\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$ and you get the first. Factor $dt$ out and you get the
second. The polar one is the parametric one with $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ substituted
in and simplified, which is a satisfying half-page of algebra where everything cancels.

**The parametric form is the honest one.** The Cartesian version cannot handle a vertical tangent
or a curve that doubles back, because those are not functions of $x$; the parametric version has no
such trouble. A circle needs two Cartesian integrals and one parametric integral.

## The integrals are usually horrible

This is the topic's practical fact. $\sqrt{1+(f')^2}$ is a radical of a square, so it almost never
has an elementary antiderivative even for simple curves. **The arc length of a parabola needs
[[Integration By Trigonometric Substitution]], and the arc length of an ellipse cannot be done at
all** in elementary terms, which is why elliptic integrals exist as their own named functions. Set
up correctly and evaluate numerically is the normal outcome, and textbook exercises are
specifically chosen from the small family where the radical happens to collapse.

Worked case where it does collapse, $y = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]$:

```
f'(x) = x^(1/2)
L = ∫₀³ √(1 + x) dx
  = [ (2/3)(1+x)^(3/2) ]₀³
  = (2/3)(8 − 1) = 14/3
```

## Surface area of a revolution

The companion formula: revolve the curve instead of measuring it, and each arc element sweeps a
band of circumference $2\pi(\text{radius})$.

$$
S = \int 2\pi\,(\text{radius})\,ds
$$

with the same $ds$ as above, radius $y$ for rotation about the $x$-axis and $x$ for the $y$-axis.
Same relationship as a cylindrical shell in [[Solids of Revolution]]: **an element of length times
the circle it travels**.

## Related

- [[Riemann Sum]] in [[CALCULUS 1]]: this is that construction with hypotenuses rather than
  rectangles
- [[Parametric Equations]] and [[Polar Coordinates]] for where the other two forms come from
- [[Solids of Revolution]] for the volume companion
- [[Line Integral]] and [[Parameterization]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]: $\int_C f\,ds$ is arc
  length with a weight on it, and $ds$ there is this $ds$
- [[Vector Norm]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]: $\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$ is the Euclidean norm
  of a displacement, so arc length is the continuous version of summing the lengths of a polyline
